newsitem.title: CHINA: Smuggled copper seen filling China breach-traders.
newsitem.headline: Smuggled copper seen filling China breach-traders.

text.p: Smuggling could be swelling China's copper imports to double the amount officially reported, accounting for the country's apparent absence from world metal markets in 1997, traders and industry sources said on Wednesday.
"(Real imports) could be double," said a European trader in Hong Kong. "It's frightening because it totally distorts consumption figures."
But Beijing's metals trading arm, China National Nonferrous Metals Import and Export Corp (CNIEC), says copper is being smuggled into China only in small amounts.
"The smuggling of copper exists in some regions, but I think the volume is still small," a CNIEC official told Reuters.
The domestic market would be upset if the amount of smuggled copper was as much as the official figure, and the government would be forced to take action, the official said.
Official customs figures show China's total imports of unrefined copper and copper products in the first two months of 1997 were up a year-on-year 28.2 percent at 77,885 tonnes.
"Official customs figures show only half of China's actual copper imports," a Shanghai metals industry source said.
"If you're paying all the duties that have to be paid to import copper, you can't compete," he said, adding that import duty and value-added tax add 20 percent to the copper price.
He said imported copper scrap could be bought in China for about $0.92 a lb, even though the C&F (cost and freight) price was $0.95.

"If you use cheap labour, say in the U.S., to separate the copper from the garbage then ship it in through the porous ports in the south (of China), you're getting duty-free imports," said the source, whose company deals in imported copper scrap.
Although international traders and producers have predicted China will need to import 300,000 tonnes of refined copper in 1997, China has not been active on the world market this year.
Traders said China's absence could partly be due to the fact that some imports were arranged as part of long-term bilateral agreements with trading partners.
As long as prices stay as high as they are -- close to $2,500 a tonne -- traders say China is unlikely to buy.
Copper prices hit one-year highs of $2,495 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange on Tuesday, before settling back to $2,493, up $19 on the day.
High imports in 1996 were believed to have left a significant carryover stockpile, reported in the Chinese press at 170,000 tonnes, or 15-to-17 percent of annual need.
But trade sources said this should have been absorbed long ago.
Nor had the recent closure of a major producer in eastern Jiangsu province had a discernible impact on the market although smelters are running at very low inventory, another Western source said.
Taicang Copper Co, which had an annual capacity of 60,000 to 70,000 tonnes of electrolytic copper, was closed in January for avoiding taxes on copper imports, customs officials said.
Traders said a few thousand tonnes of copper among assets seized from Taicang to cover unpaid taxes had yet to be accounted for.
State Statistical Bureau figures show China produced 145,900 tonnes of copper in the first two months of 1997, up 11.9 percent on the same period in 1996.
The CNIEC official said domestic copper output could basically meet demand, which has been put at around 1.2 million tonnes for 1997.
-- Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
